The Weilüe, a Chinese text composed in the early third century CE, describes the Roman Empire (Da Qin) as a vast kingdom located west of Parthia and the Great Sea, accessible by sea from Egypt in as little as two months with favorable winds [S1]. According to this source, the Roman Empire "has more than four hundred smaller cities and towns" and "extends several thousand li in all directions," with its capital city built with stone walls near the mouth of a river [S1]. A later Chinese historical text records that in 166 CE, the king of Da Qin sent envoys bearing elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn, and turtle shell, which the Chinese court noted were "neither precious nor rare," suggesting skepticism about the account [S3]. The Chinese sources thus portrayed Rome as a distant, powerful, and geographically extensive state, though one whose initial diplomatic overtures were received with some doubt about their authenticity.
